title: The Landing Page
body: You spent 9 hours on your landing page. It has a gradient, a waitlist form, and a tagline you rewrote 14 times. The waitlist has 3 signups. One is you. One is your mom. One is a bot from Lagos. You screenshot the Stripe dashboard showing $0.00 MRR and post it with the caption 'Day 1.' This is technically true.

choices.title: Share it everywhere, own the zero
choices.body: Post the $0 MRR screenshot on Twitter. Radical transparency is a brand now.

choices.title: Add more features before launching
choices.body: Nobody should see this yet. You need auth, payments, dark mode, and a blog.

choices.title: Send it to 5 friends for feedback
choices.body: You send it to five friends. Two respond. One says 'looks clean.' One asks what it does.

title: Refreshing Stripe
body: You've refreshed the Stripe dashboard 11 times today. The number hasn't changed because it can't go lower than zero. You've memorized the exact shade of gray they use for '$0.00.' You open a new tab to check Product Hunt. Then you refresh Stripe again. This is your morning routine now.

choices.title: Close the tab, build something
choices.body: You close Stripe and open your editor. Revenue comes from shipping, not staring.

choices.title: Tweet about the grind anyway
choices.body: 'Day 12 of building in public. Revenue: $0. Lessons: priceless.' Post.

choices.title: Recalculate runway for the 4th time
choices.body: You open the spreadsheet. At current burn rate you have 15 turns. Fourteen now, after the coffee.

title: Cursor Goes Hard
body: You describe your entire MVP in a Cursor prompt and hit enter. Forty seconds later you have a working app with auth, a dashboard, and a settings page. It took you three weeks to build something worse. You stare at the screen like someone who just watched a magic trick that also insulted them personally.

choices.title: Ship it, iterate later
choices.body: It works. Ship it. You'll understand the code eventually. Probably.

choices.title: Read every line, learn the patterns
choices.body: You go line by line. It takes 4 hours. You learn three things you didn't know.

choices.title: Delete it, write it yourself
choices.body: You delete the generated code. If you can't build it, you can't maintain it. Probably cope.

title: Day 47 of Building in Public
body: 'Day 47 of building in public.' You've posted this every day for 47 days. Your audience has grown from 200 to 247. That's roughly one follower per day. At this rate you'll have 1,000 followers in two years. Your product still has no users. But the thread has continuity and that feels like progress.

choices.title: Keep the streak, streaks are content
choices.body: Day 48 tomorrow. The streak IS the product. Consistency compounds. Right?

choices.title: Pivot to weekly updates instead
choices.body: Consolidate into weekly updates. Less noise, more signal. Also less dopamine.

choices.title: Ask your 247 followers what to build
choices.body: You poll your audience. 3 people respond. One wants dark mode. One wants an API. One wants you to build something completely different.

title: The Co-Working Space Dilemma
body: A co-working space in the Mission costs $400/month. That's 6.7% of your runway. But working from your apartment means you talk to nobody except your rubber duck and the DoorDash driver. The co-working space has 'community events' which means free pizza and forced networking with other people burning savings.

choices.title: Get the membership, invest in sanity
choices.body: You sign up. The free coffee alone might justify it. The humans are a bonus.

choices.title: Work from coffee shops, cheaper vibes
choices.body: $5 lattes are cheaper than $400 memberships. You become a coffee shop regular.

choices.title: Stay home, protect the runway
choices.body: Runway is life. You stay home. The rubber duck doesn't judge you.

title: The MVP Nobody Uses
body: You shipped. It's live. It works. You posted it on Twitter, Hacker News, and three Discord servers. Total signups: 7. Active users after one week: 0. The analytics dashboard — which took you two days to build — shows a single spike on launch day and then a flatline. The flatline looks like an EKG of your motivation.

choices.title: Cold DM 50 potential users
choices.body: You DM strangers on Twitter. 48 don't respond. One says 'cool.' One actually tries it.

choices.title: Pivot the whole thing, new idea
choices.body: This isn't it. Time to pivot. You have a new idea already. It's always a new idea.

choices.title: Write a postmortem thread
choices.body: You write a 'What I learned shipping to 0 users' thread. It gets more engagement than the product.

title: The Product Hunt Launch
body: You spent a week preparing your Product Hunt launch. Custom graphics. Maker comment. First comment from a friend. You wake up at midnight PST to post. By noon you have 47 upvotes and you're #18 for the day. The #1 product is an AI wrapper with a waitlist of 50,000. You are competing with funded teams using the same APIs as you.

choices.title: Hustle for upvotes all day
choices.body: You DM everyone you know. 'Can you upvote my PH launch?' Your friends comply out of love and pity.

choices.title: Focus on the users who signed up
choices.body: 47 upvotes means some people cared. Email them. Talk to them. Build for them.

choices.title: Rage-quit PH, it's a vanity metric
choices.body: Product Hunt is a beauty pageant. You close the tab and go back to building.

title: The Runway Spreadsheet
body: You have a spreadsheet with three scenarios: Optimistic, Realistic, and Oh No. Optimistic assumes you hit $1K MRR in 3 months. Realistic assumes you eat rice. Oh No assumes you move back in with your parents. You've been living in Realistic for 6 weeks. Oh No is starting to look like a plan.

choices.title: Cut all non-essential spending
choices.body: Cancel everything. Austerity era. You keep internet and Cursor. Everything else goes.

choices.title: Pick up freelance work on the side
choices.body: You take a freelance gig. It pays $2500 and buys you another month of runway.

choices.title: Ignore the spreadsheet, ship faster
choices.body: Math is the enemy of faith. You close the spreadsheet and open VS Code.

title: The Twitter Founder Clique
body: There's a group of indie hackers on Twitter who all reply to each other's posts. They all have '$X0K MRR' in their bios. They all use the word 'compounding.' You start engaging with them. One follows you back. You feel like you just got into a club where the membership fee is pretending everything is going great.

choices.title: Play the game, build the network
choices.body: You engage daily. Reply, quote-tweet, hype. It's a job but it's working.

choices.title: Focus on product, not performative posting
choices.body: You mute the timeline and go back to building. The product is the content.

choices.title: Start a Discord for founders like you
choices.body: You create a Discord for pre-revenue founders. 40 people join the first week. Most are lurkers.

title: The Y Combinator Application
body: You're filling out the YC application at 2am. 'Describe what your company does in 50 characters.' You've rewritten this 19 times. Your product is a tool that does one thing but you keep trying to make it sound like a platform. The video is due tomorrow. You look terrible on camera. You practice saying 'we' even though it's just you.

choices.title: Submit it raw, authenticity wins
choices.body: You submit it unpolished. If they want real, this is real. You are one person with a laptop.

choices.title: Polish it obsessively for a week
choices.body: You spend a week on the app. The video has jump cuts. The answers are perfect. You hear back in 6 weeks.

choices.title: Skip YC, you don't need permission
choices.body: YC is a filter, not a requirement. You close the tab and ship a feature instead.

title: The Indie Hacker Meetup
body: You go to a local indie hacker meetup. Everyone is 'building something.' Half of them are building the same AI wrapper in different colors. One guy has actual revenue and everyone treats him like a minor deity. You explain your product three times. Nobody remembers what it does. The pizza is mid.

choices.title: Exchange contacts, follow up tomorrow
choices.body: You get 5 contacts. One of them might actually be useful. You'll follow up. You actually do.

choices.title: Demo your product, own the room
choices.body: You plug your laptop into the TV and demo. Two people are impressed. One asks for the URL.

choices.title: Leave early, social battery dead
choices.body: You leave after 40 minutes. The introvert tax is real but at least you showed up.

title: The Co-Founder Question
body: Everyone keeps asking if you have a co-founder. VCs won't look at you without one. Twitter says solo founders are valid. YC says two is ideal. A friend-of-a-friend is 'looking for something.' They have opinions about equity splits and want to 'align on vision' before writing a single line of code. Red flags or green flags? You can't tell anymore.

choices.title: Stay solo, you move faster alone
choices.body: Solo founder energy. No equity splits, no alignment meetings, no drama. Just shipping.

choices.title: Take the meeting, explore it
choices.body: You grab coffee with them. They seem smart. They also seem like they want to be CEO.

choices.title: Post 'looking for a technical co-founder'
choices.body: You tweet 'looking for a technical co-founder.' 12 people DM you. 11 are non-technical.

title: The Pricing Page Paralysis
body: You've been staring at your pricing page for 3 hours. $9/month feels too cheap. $29/month feels too expensive. $19/month feels like everyone else. You look at 40 competitor pricing pages. They all use the word 'scale.' You don't have scale. You have 0 paying users and a Stripe test mode toggle you're afraid to switch.

choices.title: Just pick $19 and ship it
choices.body: $19. Done. You can change it later. The hardest part is picking a number and moving on.

choices.title: Launch free first, charge later
choices.body: Free tier to get users. You'll monetize when there's something to monetize.

choices.title: Ask Twitter what they'd pay
choices.body: You poll your followers. The results are useless. Everyone wants it free.

title: The First Dollar
body: Someone paid. $19. One person. You don't know who they are. You refresh Stripe and the number changed from $0.00 to $19.00. You screenshot it immediately. You text three people. Your hands are shaking. Nineteen dollars. This is the most meaningful nineteen dollars of your life. Your MRR is $19. You are technically a business.

choices.title: Screenshot and post the milestone
choices.body: The $19 MRR screenshot goes viral-adjacent. 200 likes. Your biggest post ever.

choices.title: Email the customer personally
choices.body: You email them a personal thank-you. They respond. They have feedback. It's good feedback.

choices.title: Reinvest it immediately into ads
choices.body: $19 into Google Ads. You get 3 clicks and 0 conversions. The machine ate your first dollar.

title: The 3am Claude Session
body: It's 3am and you're pair-programming with Claude. You've been going for 4 hours. The feature is almost done. Claude doesn't judge you. Claude doesn't need sleep. Claude just built your entire payment flow while you ate ramen. You're starting to wonder if Claude is your actual co-founder and you're the one who's replaceable.

choices.title: Ship it, credit the AI co-founder
choices.body: You ship the feature. It works. You don't tell anyone how you built it. You know.

choices.title: Go to sleep, review it tomorrow
choices.body: You save the work and close the laptop. Tomorrow-you can decide if 3am-you was a genius or a fool.

choices.title: Keep going until sunrise
choices.body: Sleep is a pre-revenue luxury. You and Claude push through until 6am. The feature ships. You crash.

title: The Competitor Who Shipped First
body: You open Twitter and see it. Someone shipped the exact same product you've been building for 3 months. They shipped it in 2 weeks. It has a better logo. It already has 500 users. The founder is 21 and says they 'had the idea last Tuesday.' You want to scream but your co-working space has an open floor plan.

choices.title: Differentiate, find your niche
choices.body: Same idea, different execution. You find the gap they missed and build into it.

choices.title: Rage-ship three features in a weekend
choices.body: Competition fuels you. You ship three features in 48 hours. Two of them work.

choices.title: Pivot entirely, start something new
choices.body: The market spoke. You close your laptop, take a walk, and come back with a new idea.

title: The Investor Coffee Chat
body: An angel investor agrees to 'grab coffee.' You prepare a pitch deck with 12 slides. They look at 2. They ask about TAM. You say a number that is technically a real number. They ask about your 'moat.' Your moat is that you work 14 hours a day. They say 'interesting' which means 'no.' The coffee costs $7 and you expense it to yourself.

choices.title: Follow up weekly until they crack
choices.body: You send follow-up emails for 6 weeks. Polite, persistent, slightly desperate.

choices.title: Forget investors, bootstrap harder
choices.body: You don't need their money. You need users. Back to building.

choices.title: Revamp the whole pitch deck
choices.body: You spend 3 days rebuilding the deck. The TAM slide now has a bigger number.

title: The Domain Name Spiral
body: You just spent $800 on a domain name. It's a .com. It's clean. It's brandable. Your product doesn't have users yet but it has a premium domain. You tell yourself this is an investment. Your runway spreadsheet disagrees. Your girlfriend asks why you just spent $800 on 'letters.' You don't have a good answer.

choices.title: Own it, premium domains signal trust
choices.body: Good domains compound. This is your brand. The $800 will pay for itself. Eventually.

choices.title: Return it, get a .co instead
choices.body: You return the domain and get the .co for $12. Nobody will notice. You will always notice.

choices.title: Flip it if the startup dies
choices.body: Worst case, you sell the domain. Domain flipping is a business. Kind of.

title: The Build vs. Buy Trap
body: You need a feature. You could use a third-party API for $50/month or build it yourself in 'a weekend.' Three weekends later you're still building it. The third-party API would have worked. But you wanted to own the stack. You always want to own the stack. The stack owns you.

choices.title: Pay for the API, ship today
choices.body: You pay. It works in 20 minutes. You feel both relieved and defeated.

choices.title: Finish building it, own your infra
choices.body: You finish your custom solution. It's worse than the API but it's yours.

choices.title: Open source your half-built version
choices.body: You clean up your code and open source it. 12 stars on GitHub. It's something.

title: The User Feedback Call
body: You have your first user feedback call. The user is nice. They say they 'love the concept.' Then they spend 40 minutes describing a completely different product they wish you'd built. Every feature request contradicts the last one. You take notes anyway. The notes say 'pivot?' with three question marks.

choices.title: Build what they asked for
choices.body: The customer is always right. You rebuild the core flow around their feedback.

choices.title: Thank them and ignore everything
choices.body: You nod, say 'great insights,' and continue building what you were building.

choices.title: Ask 10 more users the same question
choices.body: One data point is noise. You schedule 10 more calls. Three show up.

title: The SaaS Stack Tax
body: Vercel, Supabase, Resend, Stripe, Plausible, a monitoring tool, an error tracker. Your 'free tier' stack just sent you $127 in bills because you crossed three usage thresholds in the same week. You have 8 users. Your per-user cost is $15.87. This is not how business works.

choices.title: Optimize aggressively, cut costs
choices.body: You spend a day migrating to cheaper alternatives. You save $80/month.

choices.title: Ignore it, focus on growth
choices.body: Cost optimization is premature. Get users first, optimize later. Copium.

choices.title: Self-host everything on a $5 VPS
choices.body: You migrate to a single $5 DigitalOcean droplet. It's slower but it's yours.

title: The LinkedIn Bio Problem
body: Your LinkedIn says 'Founder @ Stealth.' Your parents think you work at a company called Stealth. Your ex thinks you're unemployed. Recruiters keep messaging you about senior dev roles. One of them pays more than your runway. You stare at the 'Open to Work' badge for longer than you'd like to admit.

choices.title: Update it properly, own the founder title
choices.body: You rewrite your bio. 'Building [product]. Pre-revenue. Learning everything.' Honest.

choices.title: Keep it vague, stealth is mystique
choices.body: Stealth mode protects you from judgment. Nobody can criticize what they can't see.

choices.title: Reply to the recruiter, just in case
choices.body: You reply 'not actively looking but open to chat.' Your startup doesn't need to know.

title: The Shipping Addiction
body: You shipped 4 features this week. None of them were requested. None of them solve a real problem. But each deploy gave you a tiny dopamine hit and a reason to post 'Just shipped:' with a screenshot. You are addicted to the feeling of shipping. The feeling of selling is a different drug you haven't tried yet.

choices.title: Stop shipping, start selling
choices.body: You close your editor and open your email. Time to do the thing that actually matters.

choices.title: Ship one more thing, then sell
choices.body: One more feature. Then you'll sell. You promise. The feature takes 3 days.

choices.title: Launch a changelog as content
choices.body: You turn your shipping log into a public changelog. 'Ship in public.' It's content now.

title: The Family Check-In
body: Your mom calls. 'How's the app thing going?' You say 'great' because you can't explain that you spent $6,000 of savings to build software that 8 people use and none of them pay. She asks if you need money. You say no. This is technically a lie. She says your cousin just made partner at Deloitte.

choices.title: Be honest about where things stand
choices.body: You tell her the truth. She's worried but supportive. It feels better than lying.

choices.title: Perform confidence, protect her feelings
choices.body: 'We're growing. Early days.' The 'we' is doing a lot of heavy lifting.

choices.title: Accept the money, swallow the pride
choices.body: She sends $2,000. It buys you another month. The pride costs more.

title: The Thread That Bangs
body: You write a thread about your journey as a solo founder. Raw. Honest. Slightly unhinged. '6 months ago I quit my job to build a product nobody asked for. Here's what happened.' It hits 2,000 likes. Your mentions are full of people saying 'this is so real.' Your DMs are full of people pitching you their own startups.

choices.title: Ride the wave, grow the audience
choices.body: You engage with every reply. Your followers jump by 400. You feel seen for the first time in months.

choices.title: Funnel the attention to your product
choices.body: You pin a reply linking to your product. 200 clicks. 3 signups. The conversion rate is existential.

choices.title: Log off before the dopamine addiction sets
choices.body: You close Twitter. The thread is working on its own. You don't need to watch.

title: Feature Creep Is a Lifestyle
body: Your MVP was supposed to do one thing. It now does seven things, poorly. The dashboard has tabs. TABS. You have a settings page with options nobody will ever change. You've been building for 3 months and your 'minimum' viable product is becoming a 'maximum' viable procrastination device.

choices.title: Kill features, return to core
choices.body: You delete 4 features. It hurts. The product is simpler and better. You should have done this weeks ago.

choices.title: Launch it all, let users decide
choices.body: Ship everything. Let the market tell you what matters. This is called 'discovery.'

choices.title: Hire a part-time designer to fix it
choices.body: You find a designer on Upwork. $500 for a redesign. The product finally looks like a product.

title: The Credit Card Decision
body: Your savings are at $3,000. Your burn rate is $400/turn. You could put server costs on a credit card and extend your runway by 2 months. The APR is 24.99%. Every finance person you know would say this is insane. Every founder you know has done it. The line between 'bold' and 'irresponsible' is drawn in hindsight.

choices.title: Use the card, buy more time
choices.body: You put $2,000 on the card. The runway extends. The interest starts compounding. So does the anxiety.

choices.title: Don't touch the card, stay lean
choices.body: No debt. If the startup dies, it dies clean. You'd rather fail broke than fail in debt.

choices.title: Get a part-time job instead
choices.body: You apply for a part-time dev job. 20 hours a week. It kills your momentum but saves your credit score.

title: The Hacker News Post
body: You post your Show HN. The title is carefully crafted. The first comment is someone asking why this exists when [competitor] already does it. The second comment is someone who built the same thing 'in a weekend as a joke.' The third comment is actually constructive. You cling to the third comment like a life raft.

choices.title: Engage thoughtfully with the critics
choices.body: You respond to every comment with data and humility. The thread turns positive. Barely.

choices.title: Close the tab, HN isn't your audience
choices.body: HN commenters aren't your customers. You close the tab and email your actual users.

choices.title: Rewrite your positioning overnight
choices.body: The feedback stings but it's useful. You rewrite your landing page by morning.

title: The Founder Panel You Shouldn't Attend
body: You're invited to speak on a 'founder panel' at a local startup event. The other panelists have raised $5M, $12M, and $40M. You have $3,000 in savings and a Stripe dashboard that shows $19 MRR. The moderator asks everyone to 'share their journey.' Your journey is 90 days of building alone in your apartment.

choices.title: Go, be honest, represent the 99%
choices.body: You tell the truth. 'I have $19 MRR and I'm terrified.' The audience loves it. The other panelists look uncomfortable.

choices.title: Decline, you're not ready for this
choices.body: You email back: 'Next time.' You don't feel like a founder today. Maybe tomorrow.

choices.title: Go and slightly exaggerate everything
choices.body: You round up generously. '$19 MRR' becomes 'early traction.' 'Solo' becomes 'lean team.'

title: The Burnout Warning Shot
body: You wake up and don't want to open your laptop. This has never happened before. You've been coding 12 hours a day for 3 months. Your eyes hurt. Your back hurts. You ate cereal for dinner four nights in a row. The product is 'almost there' but 'almost there' has been the status for 6 weeks. Your body is filing a formal complaint.

choices.title: Take a day off, actually rest
choices.body: You don't touch the laptop for 24 hours. You go outside. You feel human again. Briefly.

choices.title: Push through, the grind is the point
choices.body: Rest is for people with runway. You open the laptop and ship through the pain.

choices.title: Call a friend, admit you're struggling
choices.body: You call someone who isn't a founder. They remind you that you're a person, not a product.

title: The Pivot Conversation
body: You've been building for 4 months. MRR is $57. You have 12 users and 3 of them are free tier. You open a blank doc and type 'pivot ideas.' The cursor blinks. You have 6 ideas, all of which sound better than what you're doing. This is the founder trap: the grass is always greener in the next pivot.

choices.title: Commit to the current thing harder
choices.body: No more pivots. You double down. If this dies, it dies with conviction.

choices.title: Pivot to the idea with most signal
choices.body: You pick the idea that got the most 'I'd pay for that' DMs and start over.

choices.title: Talk to users before deciding anything
choices.body: You schedule 10 calls. Let the data decide, not your anxiety.

title: Your Biggest Customer Churns
body: Your best customer — the one paying $49/month, the one you built two features for — cancels. The cancellation reason says 'found alternative.' The alternative is a free AI tool that does 80% of what you do. You stare at the churn notification like it's a breakup text. It basically is.

choices.title: Email them, ask what went wrong
choices.body: You write a personal email. They respond. The feedback is brutal and useful.

choices.title: Build a moat they can't replicate
choices.body: You spend a week building features the free tool can't match. Differentiation or die.

choices.title: Accept it, focus on new acquisition
choices.body: Churn happens. You shift focus to getting new users instead of mourning old ones.

title: The 'AI Wrapper' Discourse
body: A viral post declares: 'All AI wrappers will die. OpenAI will eat you.' Your product is, if you're being honest, kind of an AI wrapper. The comments are full of people tagging products like yours. Someone tags yours specifically. 'This one's cooked lol.' 47 likes on that reply.

choices.title: Defend your product publicly
choices.body: You quote-tweet with a detailed defense of your architecture. It gets 12 likes. The damage is done.

choices.title: Ignore it, build deeper moats
choices.body: Twitter discourse isn't real. You close the app and build something the API can't do alone.

choices.title: Pivot away from the AI wrapper label
choices.body: You reposition. It's not a wrapper, it's a 'workflow automation platform.' Same product, different narrative.

title: The Mentor Appears
body: An experienced founder DMs you after seeing your building-in-public thread. They've exited twice. They offer to do a monthly call. No strings. No equity ask. Just 'paying it forward.' You're suspicious because the internet has taught you that free things are traps. But their advice on your pricing page saves you 2 weeks of experimentation.

choices.title: Accept gratefully, show up prepared
choices.body: You prep for every call. Their advice is worth more than the $6K you started with.

choices.title: Keep it casual, don't over-rely
choices.body: You chat occasionally but don't lean too hard. Independence is your identity.

choices.title: Ask them to invest
choices.body: You pitch them on angel investing. They say 'not right now.' The mentorship gets awkward.

title: The Cold Email Grind
body: You send 100 cold emails to potential customers. You personalize each one. It takes 3 days. 4 people respond. 2 of them are auto-replies. 1 says 'unsubscribe.' 1 actually wants a demo. The conversion rate is 1%. The demo is tomorrow. You're going to nail it or cry in a Starbucks bathroom.

choices.title: Nail the demo, close the deal
choices.body: The demo goes well. They sign up for the $29 plan. One customer at a time.

choices.title: Automate the cold emails with AI
choices.body: You build an AI pipeline to send personalized cold emails at scale. Efficient and slightly soulless.

choices.title: Give up on cold email, try content instead
choices.body: Cold email is dead. You start writing SEO content instead. It takes 3 months to rank.

title: The Weekend MVP That Shouldn't Exist
body: Someone on Twitter posts: 'Just built a full SaaS app in 48 hours with Claude. Auth, payments, dashboard, analytics. Deploying now.' The app does exactly what yours does. Your 3-month development timeline just became a punchline. You spent weeks on the payment integration alone. This person did it while watching Netflix. The gap between you and AI-assisted builders isn't closing. It's gone.

choices.title: Rebuild your own product in a weekend
choices.body: If they can do it in 48 hours, so can you. You rebuild from scratch with AI. It's better than version 1.

choices.title: Focus on what they can't copy: your users
choices.body: They have code. You have customers. Relationships are the moat now, not the repo.

choices.title: Spiral about your wasted months
choices.body: Three months. Gone. You could have done this in a weekend. The time cost hits harder than the money cost.

title: Ramen Profitability
body: Your MRR hits $400. This is exactly your burn rate. You are 'ramen profitable' which means you can theoretically survive forever if you never eat anything except ramen and never have a medical emergency and rent never goes up and nothing breaks. It's not a celebration. It's a ceasefire with reality.

choices.title: Celebrate, you earned this
choices.body: You tweet the milestone. You buy yourself actual food. Not ramen. A real meal. You deserve this.

choices.title: Immediately reinvest into growth
choices.body: $400 goes back into the product. Ads, tools, a product designer. Growth over comfort.

choices.title: Keep grinding, this isn't enough
choices.body: $400 isn't a business, it's a hobby that pays for itself. You need 10x this.

title: Someone Copied Your Product
body: A developer in Eastern Europe cloned your entire product. Same features, same design, half the price. They even copied your landing page copy. You find out because a user emails you: 'Is this you?' It's not you. It's a pixel-perfect clone with a different logo. Your blood pressure enters the stratosphere.

choices.title: Compete on quality and trust
choices.body: You can't stop copycats. You can out-execute them. You ship faster and build trust.

choices.title: Call them out publicly
choices.body: You post a side-by-side comparison. The indie hacker community rallies behind you. The clone takes it down.

choices.title: Send a cease and desist via AI lawyer
choices.body: You use an AI legal tool to draft a C&D. It costs $50 and looks 60% legitimate.

title: The AI Runway Math
body: You sit down to recalculate runway and realize something strange. AI tools cost you $2,100/month — Cursor, Claude, Midjourney, Vercel AI. But they replaced what would have been $30,000/month in contractors. You're a solo founder running a team-of-ten operation for the cost of a used Honda payment. The leverage is obscene. The dependency is terrifying.

choices.title: Lean in, maximize the leverage
choices.body: You cancel the one contractor you still have. AI does everything now. Runway extends by 8 months.

choices.title: Diversify your AI tools, reduce risk
choices.body: You spread across multiple AI providers so no single price hike kills you. Smart. Paranoid. Both.

choices.title: Keep some humans in the loop
choices.body: You keep the designer on retainer. Humans notice things AI doesn't. Insurance against slop.

title: The Acqui-Hire Offer
body: A mid-stage startup offers to 'acqui-hire' you. They like your product. They like your skills. They'll give you a senior title, $180K salary, and 0.2% equity. Your product gets absorbed into their platform. The offer is financial salvation wrapped in creative death. Your runway has 6 weeks left.

choices.title: Take it, survival isn't selling out
choices.body: You accept. The salary is real. The equity might vest. Your product lives on, sort of.

choices.title: Negotiate harder, you have leverage
choices.body: You counter. More equity, a product lead title, and creative control. They come back at 0.4%.

choices.title: Decline and keep building
choices.body: You say no. Six weeks of runway. The clock is loud. But the product is yours.

title: Outshipped by a Teenager
body: AI agents can now build, deploy, and iterate on SaaS products autonomously. A 14-year-old just shipped a competitor to your product using nothing but voice commands and an agent swarm. It took 45 minutes. You see the Product Hunt launch. It has 800 upvotes. The kid's bio says 'building is easy, distribution is the game.' The 14-year-old understood the new rules before you did.

choices.title: Use agents yourself, level up
choices.body: If you can't beat the agents, use the agents. You integrate AI agents into your workflow.

choices.title: Go deeper on the human layer
choices.body: Agents can't do customer empathy. You go deep on the human problems your product solves.

choices.title: Panic-ship 5 features in a weekend
choices.body: You enter hyperbuild mode. 48 hours, no sleep, 5 features. Three of them break in production.

title: VCs Changed the Question
body: You take an investor coffee meeting. They don't ask 'what's your moat?' anymore. They ask: 'What can't AI replicate about this in 24 hours?' You open your mouth. Nothing comes out. Your product is good. Your code is solid. Your design is clean. But an AI agent could rebuild all of it before your coffee gets cold. The investor sips their latte and waits.

choices.title: Pitch your network and distribution
choices.body: 'My moat is 2,000 followers who trust me and 120 customers who stay.' The investor nods. It's not nothing.

choices.title: Admit you don't have one yet
choices.body: Radical honesty: 'I don't have a moat. I have speed and taste. That might not be enough.' They respect it.

choices.title: Pivot the pitch to a harder problem
choices.body: You pivot mid-meeting to a problem that requires domain expertise and human judgment. Risky but differentiated.

title: The Viral Moment
body: You post a demo video of your product. You didn't think it was special. It gets 50,000 views. Your waitlist goes from 40 to 4,000 overnight. Your server goes down. Your Stripe dashboard gets its first real spike. You are briefly, accidentally, internet famous. Your mom texts: 'I saw your app on the news????'

choices.title: Capitalize fast, convert the traffic
choices.body: You fix the server, send a welcome email blast, and convert 200 signups into paying users.

choices.title: Stay calm, don't let hype distort focus
choices.body: You ignore the vanity metrics and focus on the 200 people who actually need your product.

choices.title: Post a behind-the-scenes thread
choices.body: You ride the wave with a 'how I built this' thread. It doubles the engagement.

title: The Post-Viral Crash
body: The viral moment faded. Your traffic is back to normal. The 4,000 waitlist signups? 90% never came back. The 10% who did found bugs. Your support inbox is full of complaints from people who tried your product once and expected it to be perfect. You went from 'nobody knows me' to 'everybody has opinions' in 72 hours.

choices.title: Fix every bug, earn the retention
choices.body: You spend 2 weeks fixing bugs and responding to every support email. Retention improves.

choices.title: Ignore the noise, build for power users
choices.body: The complainers aren't your users. You focus on the 12 people who love the product.

choices.title: Try to go viral again immediately
choices.body: You chase the high. You post daily trying to recreate the magic. It doesn't work.

title: Your Only Competitive Advantage
body: You're in the shower when it hits you. Your product's only competitive advantage is that YOU thought of it first. That's it. The code is replicable. The design is replicable. The features are replicable. The only non-replicable thing was the initial insight, and AI brainstorming tools are now generating 1,000 startup ideas per minute. Your shower thought has a shelf life of about six hours.

choices.title: Move faster than the idea generators
choices.body: Ideas are cheap. Execution with context is expensive. You ship three iterations before anyone copies the concept.

choices.title: Build relationships as the real moat
choices.body: You call your top 10 customers by name. You know their problems. An AI can't replicate two years of trust.

choices.title: Accept commoditization, compete on brand
choices.body: If the product is replicable, the person behind it isn't. You invest in being the face, not the feature set.

title: The Startup Conference
body: You're at a startup conference. Your badge says 'Founder.' Everyone else's badge also says 'Founder.' 80% of them have the same glazed, caffeinated look. The keynote speaker raised $100M and talks about 'doing things that don't scale.' You are doing things that don't scale because you can't afford things that scale.

choices.title: Network aggressively, collect every card
choices.body: You talk to 30 people. You forget 25 of them immediately. But 5 conversations matter.

choices.title: Skip the talks, hack in the lobby
choices.body: You set up in the lobby with your laptop and code. Three people ask what you're building.

choices.title: Leave early, conferences are theater
choices.body: You leave at 2pm. The ROI of a conference is negative. You go home and ship.

title: The Pricing Experiment
body: You raise your price from $19 to $49. Three customers cancel immediately. Two new customers sign up. Your MRR goes up by $21. You feel sick about the cancellations and ecstatic about the new signups. This is what 'price elasticity' feels like when you have 15 customers and every single one has a face.

choices.title: Keep the new price, trust the math
choices.body: $49 is the right price. The people who pay $49 are better customers. You're learning.

choices.title: Grandfather the old customers in
choices.body: You email the cancellations and offer the old price. Two come back. Loyalty is expensive.

choices.title: A/B test everything obsessively
choices.body: You set up 4 pricing tiers and an A/B test. The data will take 3 months to be meaningful.

title: The 48-Hour Competitor
body: A competitor launches. It was built by one person with AI in 48 hours. It's better than yours. Better design, better onboarding, better copy. The founder has no domain expertise, no customer relationships, no history in the space. They just described what they wanted and an AI built it. Your 8 months of grinding feels like bringing a knife to a drone strike.

choices.title: Study their product, steal what works
choices.body: You sign up for their product. You take notes. You ship three improvements in a week.

choices.title: Compete on depth, not polish
choices.body: Their product is beautiful and shallow. Yours is ugly and deep. You double down on power features.

choices.title: Reach out, suggest a merger
choices.body: You DM them. 'Your design, my customers, our product.' They say 'interesting.' It goes nowhere.

title: The Meta-Project Trap
body: You're building a tool to help you build your product. It's a meta-project. A side project of a side project. The tool is actually more interesting than the product. You're now spending more time on the tool than on the thing that's supposed to make money. You are a recursive founder.

choices.title: Kill the tool, focus on the product
choices.body: You delete the repo. It hurts. But the product needs you more than the tool does.

choices.title: Launch the tool as a separate product
choices.body: You ship the tool. It gets more users in a week than your main product got in 3 months.

choices.title: Open source the tool, keep the product
choices.body: You open source the tool and keep the product closed. Best of both worlds. Maybe.

title: The $1K MRR Milestone
body: $1,000 MRR. You screenshot it 4 times from different angles. You've been building for 7 months. $1K/month is not enough to live on. It's not enough to prove anything. But it's $1,000 that strangers give you every month for something you made. You don't know how to feel. Proud? Scared? Both? You post it anyway.

choices.title: Post the milestone, inspire others
choices.body: The $1K MRR post gets 3,000 likes. People call you an inspiration. The imposter syndrome doubles.

choices.title: Keep it private, stay humble
choices.body: You don't post it. You celebrate quietly. The product speaks for itself.

choices.title: Immediately set sights on $5K MRR
choices.body: $1K is base camp. You set a new target and plan the features to get there.

title: The Fake Investor
body: Someone DMs you claiming to be a VC partner at a fund you've never heard of. They love your product. They want to invest $250K. All you need to do is pay a $2,000 'due diligence fee.' Your gut says scam. Your runway says please. Their LinkedIn has 47 connections and was created 3 weeks ago.

choices.title: Ignore it, trust your gut
choices.body: You block them. The $250K was never real. Your gut saved you $2,000.

choices.title: Investigate, maybe it's real
choices.body: You spend 3 hours researching them. It's a scam. But the hope was nice while it lasted.

choices.title: Fall for it, desperation is expensive
choices.body: You pay the fee. The 'investor' disappears. You feel stupid. You are $2,000 lighter.

title: The Newsletter Pivot
body: Your product has 20 paying users but your Twitter has 2,000 followers. You start a newsletter about building in public. The newsletter gets more engagement than the product. You start to wonder: are you a founder or a content creator? Is the newsletter the product? Is the product just content for the newsletter?

choices.title: Double down on the newsletter
choices.body: You go all-in on the newsletter. Sponsorships start coming in. The product becomes secondary.

choices.title: Use the newsletter to drive product signups
choices.body: Every issue funnels to the product. The conversion rate is 2%. It's something.

choices.title: Abandon the newsletter, focus on product
choices.body: Content is a distraction. You stop the newsletter and ship 3 features that week.

title: The Mentor Gets Real
body: Your mentor looks at your metrics and says something you didn't want to hear: 'I think you should consider getting a job.' Not quit forever — just get stable while you figure this out. They're not wrong. Your runway is 2 months. Your MRR covers coffee. The advice is good. It tastes like failure.

choices.title: Take the advice, get stable first
choices.body: You start interviewing while maintaining the product. It's exhausting but responsible.

choices.title: Push back, ask for more time
choices.body: 'Give me 3 more months.' Your mentor nods. The clock resets. The pressure doubles.

choices.title: Cut off the mentor, they don't get it
choices.body: You stop taking their calls. They don't understand your vision. Nobody does.

title: The Health Crash
body: Your back gave out. Literally. Three months of 14-hour days in a chair that cost $60 on Amazon. The doctor says 'repetitive strain' and 'posture' and 'stress' like these are choices you made. They were. The prescription is rest. Rest costs money you don't have because you're not making money because you're working 14-hour days.

choices.title: Take a week off, actually heal
choices.body: You step away for a week. The product doesn't die. You're surprised.

choices.title: Buy an ergonomic setup, keep going
choices.body: You spend $400 on a real chair and a standing desk. It helps. Somewhat.

choices.title: Ignore it, ibuprofen and vibes
choices.body: You take 4 Advil and keep coding. The back gets worse. Your body keeps the score.

title: The Slop Moment
body: You shipped 5 features this week using nothing but AI generation. Fast. Efficient. Your users complain that the product 'feels different.' One says 'the copy reads like it was written by a robot.' It was. Another says the new features feel 'generic.' They are. You've optimized for speed and accidentally shipped mediocrity at scale.

choices.title: Slow down, add the human touch back
choices.body: You rewrite every piece of copy by hand. It takes 3 days. The product feels like yours again.

choices.title: Double down, speed is the moat
choices.body: Users will adapt. You keep shipping fast. Quantity has a quality all its own.

choices.title: Hire a writer for $500 to humanize it
choices.body: You hire a human writer. The product copy improves. Your wallet shrinks.

title: The Relationship Casualty
body: Your partner says: 'I feel like I'm dating your laptop.' They're right. You've canceled three dinner plans for 'urgent bugs.' You work through every weekend. The startup is your first thought in the morning and your last thought at night. They didn't sign up for this. The relationship is another burn rate you forgot to model.

choices.title: Set boundaries, protect the relationship
choices.body: You establish no-laptop hours. 7pm to 10pm is human time. It's hard but necessary.

choices.title: Choose the startup, accept the cost
choices.body: You have a conversation. It doesn't go well. The startup survives. The relationship doesn't.

choices.title: Promise to change, mean it this time
choices.body: You promise to change. You mean it. For two weeks. Then a feature ships and you disappear again.

title: Your Content Got Scraped
body: An AI model used your blog posts as training data. You know because someone asks the model about your product's category and it quotes your writing verbatim — without attribution, without a link, without a care. Your content is now someone else's training data and someone else's chatbot response. Welcome to the content commons.

choices.title: Rage-post about it, get engagement
choices.body: You write an angry thread about AI training data. It goes semi-viral. Nothing changes.

choices.title: Accept it, your content is out there
choices.body: The internet took your content. You can't unfeed the model. You keep writing anyway.

choices.title: Add a paywall, gate future content
choices.body: You put your best content behind a paywall. Engagement drops. Revenue from content: $12/month.

title: The Technical Debt Bomb
body: You've been shipping fast for 8 months. The codebase is held together by duct tape and Claude-generated code you never refactored. A simple feature change now takes 3 days because everything depends on everything. You built a Jenga tower and every feature request is pulling from the bottom.

choices.title: Stop shipping, refactor for 2 weeks
choices.body: You take 2 weeks to refactor. No new features. Your MRR flatlines. The code is cleaner.

choices.title: Keep shipping, deal with it later
choices.body: Tech debt is tomorrow's problem. Today's problem is revenue. You keep shipping.

choices.title: Ask AI to rewrite the whole thing
choices.body: You prompt Claude to rewrite your codebase from scratch. It takes a weekend. The new version is cleaner but the migration breaks three things.

title: The Trough of Disillusionment
body: You're in the trough. The excitement of starting is gone. The validation of success hasn't arrived. You're in the middle — the boring, terrifying middle where nothing exciting happens and everything is slightly broken. Your MRR is flat. Your motivation is flat. You Google 'when to quit your startup' at 2am.

choices.title: Talk to other founders, you're not alone
choices.body: You join a founder support group. Everyone is in the trough. The solidarity helps.

choices.title: Set a quit date, give yourself a deadline
choices.body: If you don't hit $3K MRR in 3 months, you get a job. The deadline clarifies everything.

choices.title: Push through on pure stubbornness
choices.body: You don't quit. Not because it's smart. Because you can't. Stubbornness is a resource.

title: The Co-Founder Breakup
body: You finally found a co-founder 3 months ago. It's over. They want to pivot. You don't. They wrote 200 lines of code and have opinions about 2,000. The equity split conversation gets ugly. They threaten to fork the repo. You realize why everyone warns about co-founder conflicts. The breakup is messier than any romantic one you've had.

choices.title: Buy them out cleanly, move on
choices.body: You offer them a clean exit. It costs money you don't have but it's worth the peace.

choices.title: Fight for the repo and the name
choices.body: It's your product. You built it. The legal threats fly. It takes weeks.

choices.title: Let them fork it, you'll outbuild them
choices.body: They fork the repo. You don't care. You'll ship faster, build better, and move on.

title: Claude Can Build Your Whole Product
body: You realize that Claude can now build your entire product from a single prompt. Not just pieces — the whole thing. Auth, dashboard, payments, the feature you spent 2 weeks on. All of it. In minutes. You are a founder whose competitive advantage was 'I can code fast' and the machines just lapped you. What do you even do now?

choices.title: Become the taste layer, not the code layer
choices.body: AI writes the code. You provide the taste, the vision, the curation. That's the job now.

choices.title: Build something AI can't easily replicate
choices.body: You go deep on a problem that requires domain expertise and human judgment.

choices.title: Existential crisis, take a walk
choices.body: You close everything and walk for 2 hours. The sidewalk doesn't require an API key.

title: The Investor Who Ghosted
body: You had a great investor meeting. They said 'this is really compelling.' They asked for a data room. You spent 3 days preparing the data room. You sent it. Then: silence. One follow-up. Silence. Two follow-ups. Silence. Three weeks later they invest in a competitor. They never tell you. You find out on Twitter.

choices.title: Move on, VC is a volume game
choices.body: You add them to the 'ghosted by' list and keep pitching. Rejection is a feature, not a bug.

choices.title: Send one final honest email
choices.body: 'I noticed you invested in [competitor]. No hard feelings. Feedback would help.' They actually respond.

choices.title: Swear off investors entirely
choices.body: Bootstrap forever. You don't need their money or their games. The product will fund itself. Maybe.

title: The Geo-Arbitrage Play
body: Your lease is up. SF rent is $2,800. You could move to Lisbon, Medellin, or Bali and pay $800. Your product is online. Your customers are everywhere. Your social life is on Twitter. The only thing keeping you here is inertia and a WeWork membership. The flight to Lisbon costs less than one month's rent.

choices.title: Move abroad, extend the runway
choices.body: You book a one-way to Lisbon. Runway extends by 6 months. You join the digital nomad meme.

choices.title: Stay, community matters more than savings
choices.body: You renew the lease. The local connections are worth the premium. Probably.

choices.title: Compromise with a cheaper US city
choices.body: Austin. Denver. Boise. Somewhere with WiFi and rent that doesn't require investors.

title: Teaching What You Know
body: Someone asks you to give a talk at a bootcamp about indie hacking. The pay is $200. You say yes because $200 is $200 and also because explaining your journey to beginners makes you feel like you know what you're doing. The students ask questions you can't answer. You realize teaching is learning with a microphone.

choices.title: Start a course, monetize the knowledge
choices.body: You create a small course about shipping products solo. 40 people buy it. $800 in revenue.

choices.title: Mentor a few students directly
choices.body: You take on 3 mentees. No charge. Watching them ship feels better than your own MRR.

choices.title: Decline, you're not qualified yet
choices.body: You say no. You don't feel like a teacher. You still feel like a student pretending.

title: First Taste of Lifestyle Creep
body: MRR hit $2K. You're not rich but you're not panicking. You buy an oat milk latte without checking your bank account. You upgrade your Spotify to family. You eat out twice in a week. It felt like breathing. Then you check your runway spreadsheet and realize you spent an extra $400 this month. Comfort is expensive.

choices.title: Lock it down, stay hungry
choices.body: You go back to austerity mode. The latte era is over. Back to drip coffee.

choices.title: Allow small comforts, they sustain you
choices.body: You budget $200/month for 'not losing your mind.' It's an investment in sanity.

choices.title: Reinvest every dollar into growth
choices.body: $2K goes straight back into the product. Ads, tools, a VA. Growth over comfort, always.

title: $5K MRR and Zero Moat
body: $5,000 MRR. The product works. People pay for it. But last week a YC batch launched with 200 companies — each founded by a single person with AI. Average valuation: $5M. Average build time: one weekend. Your 14 months of grinding produced what a fresh grad can now replicate before lunch. The question isn't 'can this scale?' The question is 'why does this exist?'

choices.title: Hire your first contractor
choices.body: You hire a part-time support person. $1,500/month. You sleep again. The humans are the moat now.

choices.title: Automate everything with AI agents
choices.body: You replace support, marketing, and half of engineering with agents. Headcount: you. Capability: a small team.

choices.title: Let response times slip, focus on product
choices.body: You answer slower. Some customers complain. Most don't notice. You ship more features.

title: 1,000 Clones in a Week
body: You launched a major feature on Monday. By Friday there are 1,000 clones. Not copies — pixel-perfect reproductions, auto-generated by AI scraper bots that monitor Product Hunt and rebuild anything that gets traction. Your feature is now a commodity before your launch tweet stops getting impressions. The moat isn't technology. It's marketing. And you're one person.

choices.title: Double down on community and brand
choices.body: Your brand is your moat now. You invest in community, content, and relationships. Code is free.

choices.title: Ship faster than anyone can clone
choices.body: Speed is the only moat. You ship daily. The clones are always 24 hours behind. For now.

choices.title: Open source and make cloning pointless
choices.body: If everyone can clone you, own the cloning. Open source the code, sell the hosting.

title: Agents Are Replacing SaaS
body: The prediction came true: AI agents are replacing SaaS products. Why pay $49/month for a tool when an agent can do the same thing for free? Your product category is being eaten alive. Three competitors shut down this month. Your churn rate doubled. Users aren't leaving for a better product — they're leaving for no product. The agent just does it.

choices.title: Pivot to an agent-native product
choices.body: If agents are the platform, build for agents. You rebuild your product as agent infrastructure.

choices.title: Go premium, serve the humans who remain
choices.body: Some people still want human-designed tools. You go upmarket. $149/month. Fewer customers, higher trust.

choices.title: Accept the end, wind down gracefully
choices.body: You email your customers. 'We're shutting down in 60 days.' The responses are kinder than you expected.

title: Solo Founders Get Funded Now
body: Investors stopped funding teams. The new thesis: 'AI-native solo founders' are more capital-efficient than teams of 2+. A VC tweets: 'If you need a co-founder in 2026, you don't understand the tools.' Your solo founder status went from red flag to green flag overnight. VCs are sliding into YOUR DMs now. Two years of being told 'solo founders can't scale' and the market just flipped.

choices.title: Take a meeting, hear them out
choices.body: You take three meetings. One offers $500K at $5M. Real money. Real terms. The bootstrapper in you screams.

choices.title: Stay bootstrapped, the attention is validation enough
choices.body: You decline politely. The VC attention validates what you always knew: solo works.

choices.title: Negotiate from strength for the first time
choices.body: You counter every term. Higher valuation. No board seat. Founder-friendly everything. They agree.

title: Revenue Is Easy Now
body: $10,000 a month. It took 18 months. But here's the thing nobody warned you about: revenue is easy now. AI handles acquisition, onboarding, retention. Every solo founder has revenue. Differentiation is impossible. You're one of 10,000 AI wrappers making $5K-$15K/month. The floor rose but the ceiling dropped. Everyone is ramen profitable and nobody is winning.

choices.title: Go vertical, niche down hard
choices.body: You pick one industry. Plumbers. AI-powered plumber scheduling. Nobody else bothered. Revenue doubles.

choices.title: Build a portfolio of micro-products
choices.body: If one product maxes out at $10K, run five of them. You become a product studio of one.

choices.title: Take your first real paycheck
choices.body: You pay yourself $4,000 and put $6,000 back into the business. A salary. From yourself. To yourself.

title: The 13-Year-Old's Series A
body: A 13-year-old's AI-built competitor just raised a Series A. $4 million. The pitch deck was AI-generated. The product was AI-built. The financial model was AI-projected. The kid did one thing: they had the idea and the audacity to execute. The VC who funded them tweeted: 'Age is irrelevant. Taste is everything.' You are 29 and questioning everything.

choices.title: Learn from the kid, adapt
choices.body: You study their approach. Zero ego, pure execution. You adopt their playbook. It works better than yours.

choices.title: Compete on experience and depth
choices.body: A 13-year-old can build fast. They can't understand enterprise pain points. You go deeper.

choices.title: Spiral about age and relevance
choices.body: You're 29. In AI years, that's ancient. The productivity gap between you and a kid with an agent is closing.

title: The Word 'Startup' Means Nothing
body: The concept of 'startup' is dying. When anyone can build anything in hours, the barrier to entry is zero. Your Uber driver launched a SaaS last Tuesday. Your dentist has a micro-product on the side. The word 'founder' used to mean something specific. Now it means 'person with a laptop and an idea,' which is everyone. You're not special anymore. Neither is your company.

choices.title: Redefine founder around longevity
choices.body: Anyone can start. Not everyone persists. Your 18 months of iteration IS the differentiator now.

choices.title: Drop the label entirely
choices.body: You stop calling yourself a founder. You're a person who makes things. The label doesn't matter.

choices.title: Lean into the absurdity
choices.body: If everyone's a founder, nothing means anything. You tweet 'I'm a founder of founders' and get 5K likes.

title: Teams of Two Are 'Bloated' Now
body: A VC wrote a viral thread: 'In 2026, a team of 2 is bloated. If you need a co-founder, your AI stack is weak.' They funded 40 solo founders this quarter and zero teams. Your friend who spent months finding a co-founder just got told their company is 'over-staffed.' The future is one person, infinite AI, zero overhead. You're already there. So are 50,000 others.

choices.title: Ride the solo founder wave
choices.body: The narrative fits you perfectly. You lean into it. Speaking invites arrive. You become a case study.

choices.title: Quietly hire anyway, humans matter
choices.body: You hire a part-time human. Don't tell the VCs. Some things still need a person.

choices.title: Question the whole narrative
choices.body: Solo founder worship is just cost optimization with a brand. You write a counterpoint. It gets ratio'd.

title: What Does 'Founder' Even Mean?
body: You defined yourself as a 'builder.' AI builds better. You defined yourself as a 'coder.' AI codes faster. You defined yourself as a 'shipping machine.' AI ships infinitely. Every identity you built your self-worth around is now a commodity skill. The thing that made you special is now free. What does 'founder' mean when founding costs nothing?

choices.title: Redefine around taste and judgment
choices.body: AI can build anything. Knowing WHAT to build is the human skill. You become a taste curator.

choices.title: Have the crisis, feel it fully
choices.body: You sit with the emptiness for a week. No building. No shipping. Just sitting with who you are without the labels.

choices.title: Build something AI genuinely can't
choices.body: You start a project rooted in lived experience and relationships. Messy, human, unscalable. Yours.

title: The AI Co-Founder
body: You realize your AI tools have effectively become your co-founder. Claude writes your code, generates your marketing copy, handles your customer support drafts, and helps you think through strategy. Your human co-founder search is over because you found one that works 24/7, never wants equity, and never has a bad day. But last week Claude made a strategic suggestion that was better than anything you'd have thought of. That's the part that keeps you up at night.

choices.title: Lean in, this is the future
choices.body: You restructure your workflow around AI. You become the operator, not the builder. The loneliness is new.

choices.title: Maintain human touch, AI is a tool
choices.body: AI helps but doesn't decide. You keep humans in the loop for everything that matters.

choices.title: Get uncomfortable about what this means
choices.body: If AI is your co-founder, what are you? The question keeps you up at night. The answer keeps changing.

title: The Acquisition Offer
body: A company offers to buy your product for $150K. After 14 months of building, $150K feels like a fortune and an insult simultaneously. But here's the new math: they could rebuild your product with AI in a week for $500. They're not buying the code. They're buying the customers and your name. The premium isn't technology anymore. It's trust.

choices.title: Take the money, start something new
choices.body: You sell. $150K lands in your account. You feel relief and grief in equal measure.

choices.title: Counter at $500K for the brand
choices.body: You counter: 'The code is worthless. The brand is worth $500K.' They pause. They come back at $300K.

choices.title: Decline, the trust is worth more
choices.body: If trust is the asset, selling it destroys it. You keep the brand. You keep the relationships.

title: The Sabbatical Temptation
body: You haven't taken a real break in 18 months. Not a weekend — a real break. Two weeks minimum. No laptop. No Stripe dashboard. No support tickets. Your body wants it. Your mind needs it. But here's the new fear: if you stop for two weeks, AI might advance enough to make your entire product category obsolete by the time you return. The treadmill is accelerating.

choices.title: Take two weeks off, trust the product
choices.body: You set up auto-responders and disappear for 14 days. The product survives. The world didn't end. You return human.

choices.title: Take a long weekend, compromise
choices.body: 4 days. You check Slack twice. It's not a real break but it's more than you've had.

choices.title: Can't afford to stop, keep grinding
choices.body: Breaks are for people whose industries aren't being disrupted weekly. You push through.

title: The Ethical Line
body: A larger competitor asks you to integrate your product with their platform. During the process, you discover they're using AI to fabricate customer testimonials and fake usage metrics to investors. It's fraud. Your 200 users would be associated with this. You could stay quiet — the partnership is worth $3K/month. Or you could say something and lose everything.

choices.title: Blow the whistle, protect your users
choices.body: You publish a blog post detailing what you found. The competitor threatens legal action. Your users rally behind you.

choices.title: Walk away quietly, no partnership
choices.body: You decline the partnership without explanation. They move on. Your users are safe. Nobody knows why.

choices.title: Stay quiet, take the money
choices.body: You integrate. The money flows. You don't look at their practices again. The compromise sits in your stomach.

title: The Housing Squeeze
body: Your landlord raises rent by 30%. Your MRR covers your old rent. It does not cover your new rent. You could move somewhere cheaper but your entire routine is built around this neighborhood. Uprooting your life to save $800/month feels like admitting the startup isn't working. Meanwhile a founder in Lagos with the same product and zero overhead is eating your lunch.

choices.title: Move to a cheaper place, adapt
choices.body: You move. The new place is smaller and farther from everything. But the math works.

choices.title: Stay, make the product earn the rent
choices.body: You stay and use the financial pressure as motivation. Ship harder. Sell harder.

choices.title: Go nomad, join the geo-arbitrage class
choices.body: No apartment. Airbnbs, co-living, friend's couches. Your overhead drops to nearly zero.

title: The Cancellation
body: You tweeted something about AI replacing founders. It was nuanced in your head and inflammatory on the timeline. Quote tweets multiply. Strangers are writing threads about you. Someone found your product and is leaving 1-star reviews. Your brand — the thing you spent 18 months building, the only moat you have left — is being dismantled in real time.

choices.title: Apologize, clarify, ride it out
choices.body: You post a thoughtful clarification. Half the mob accepts it. The other half quotes it angrily. It fades in 72 hours.

choices.title: Delete the tweet, go dark
choices.body: You delete everything and go offline for a week. When you come back, the internet has moved on.

choices.title: Double down, own the controversy
choices.body: You stand by the tweet. Some customers leave. New ones arrive. Your brand now has an edge.

title: The Comeback
body: After the crisis you're rebuilding. The MRR took a hit but the product is still alive. You have fewer users but they're the right users. The existential dread faded into a quiet determination. The new game is clear: technology is free, distribution is hard, trust is everything. You've been knocked down before. This time you get up differently.

choices.title: Rebuild quietly, let the work speak
choices.body: No more building in public. You go dark and ship for 3 months. When you resurface, the product is unrecognizable.

choices.title: Document the comeback, inspire others
choices.body: You write about what went wrong and how you recovered. The vulnerability resonates more than any product launch.

choices.title: Pivot entirely, new product, new you
choices.body: The old product is a chapter. You start something new with everything you learned. Faster this time.

title: The Indie Workers Collective
body: A group of indie hackers is forming a collective. Shared health insurance, group buying power for AI tools, mutual support during crises. It's not a union — it's a 'collective' because solo founders don't do unions. But 50,000 solo founders all facing the same existential threats might need solidarity more than independence. The annual fee is $500.

choices.title: Join, solidarity is strength
choices.body: You join. The health insurance alone saves you $200/month. Collective bargaining with AI providers saves more.

choices.title: Stay independent, you're fine alone
choices.body: You don't need a collective. You're a founder. Independence is the point.

choices.title: Help organize it, take a leadership role
choices.body: You help build the collective's infrastructure. It becomes another project. But a meaningful one.

title: The Debt Reckoning
body: The credit card debt is $8,000. The minimum payment is $200/month. At this rate you'll be paying it off for 7 years. The interest alone is eating your MRR gains. Every time you check the balance, a small part of your founding story rewrites itself from 'bold bet' to 'financial mistake.' The line between those two things was always thinner than LinkedIn suggests.

choices.title: Pay it all off from MRR savings
choices.body: You allocate 3 months of profit to debt. It hurts but the freedom is worth it.

choices.title: Balance transfer, buy time
choices.body: You move it to a 0% APR card. 18 months to pay it off. The timer starts.

choices.title: Ignore it, focus on revenue growth
choices.body: The debt will feel smaller if revenue grows. You focus on MRR. The debt stays.

title: Distribution Is the Only Game
body: The winners aren't technical anymore. They're interesting, trustworthy, or famous. A former reality TV star launched an AI product and hit $100K MRR in a week. A TikTok creator's SaaS has more users than yours despite being objectively worse. Distribution beats product. Celebrity beats craft. You built the better mousetrap and the internet doesn't care because the other founder has 2 million followers.

choices.title: Become a personality, not just a builder
choices.body: You start showing your face. Video content. Podcasts. Being a person, not just a product. It feels fake. It works.

choices.title: Partner with someone who has distribution
choices.body: You find a creator with an audience and offer them a revenue share. Their reach, your product.

choices.title: Accept the niche, serve your 200 people well
choices.body: You don't need millions. You need 200 people who trust you and pay you $50/month. That's a life.

title: Rock Bottom
body: MRR dropped to $800. Your savings are gone. You owe $5K on a credit card. Your biggest customer churned because an AI agent replaced your product entirely. You're eating rice for the third night in a row. The Stripe dashboard is a crime scene. You open Twitter and see a 15-year-old raise $10M for an AI company they built in a weekend. You close the laptop. It stays closed for 3 days.

choices.title: Accept it, start the rebuild
choices.body: You hit bottom. There's only one direction from here. You start planning the comeback.

choices.title: Get a job, save what's left
choices.body: You apply for jobs. The interviews feel strange after 18 months of freedom. A paycheck arrives. You exhale.

choices.title: Ask for help, finally
choices.body: You text 5 friends: 'I'm not okay.' Three respond immediately. You aren't alone. You forgot.

title: Big Tech Ate Your Lunch
body: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all launching products in your exact space. Not wrappers — actual first-party products. They have infinite engineers, zero customer acquisition cost, and built-in distribution to millions. You have a Vercel deployment and determination. The David vs. Goliath narrative is nice until Goliath shows up with 10,000 Goliaths. Each one built by AI in a day.

choices.title: Go niche, find the gap they won't fill
choices.body: Big companies can't serve every niche. You find yours and dig in. The gap is small but it's yours.

choices.title: Become a distribution layer for their APIs
choices.body: You pivot to being the UX layer on top of their APIs. The value is in the workflow, not the model.

choices.title: Shut down and join one of them
choices.body: If you can't beat them, join them. You apply. Your founder experience is worth $250K to them.

title: The Enterprise Pivot
body: A Fortune 500 company wants to use your product. They need SSO, SOC 2 compliance, a contract review, and a dedicated Slack channel. They'll pay $5,000/month. Building enterprise features will take 3 months and you'll become an enterprise company. But enterprise companies have one customer who controls their destiny. One person, one customer, one point of failure.

choices.title: Go enterprise, chase the bag
choices.body: You build SSO in two weeks with AI. SOC 2 takes longer. But the contract signs. You're an enterprise company now.

choices.title: Stay indie, enterprise isn't your vibe
choices.body: You decline politely. Enterprise kills indie energy. You'd rather have 200 happy individuals.

choices.title: White-label it, let someone else do enterprise
choices.body: You find a partner to resell your product to enterprises. They handle compliance. You handle product.

title: TechCrunch Wants to Talk
body: A TechCrunch reporter emails asking about your product. Not because of your product specifically — because you're a case study for the 'solo AI founder' trend piece. They want to write about how one person with AI tools can run what used to require a 20-person company. You're not the story. The phenomenon is the story. You're the anecdote.

choices.title: Nail the interview, ride the PR wave
choices.body: The article publishes. Your traffic spikes 5x. You're the face of solo founding. The scrutiny follows.

choices.title: Stay cautious, don't overhype
choices.body: You keep it real in the interview. The article is balanced. The traffic is modest. But it's honest.

choices.title: Decline, you don't want the attention
choices.body: You say no. Being a case study for a trend means being disposable when the trend dies.

title: Open Source Takes Off
body: Your open-source project hit 5,000 GitHub stars. Contributors are submitting PRs. Companies are using it in production. But here's the weird part: AI agents are also contributing. Automated PRs with perfect code, no human attached. Your open-source community is becoming half-human, half-machine. The contributions are good. The uncanny valley is real.

choices.title: Launch a managed service around it
choices.body: You launch a hosted version. $49/month. 50 companies sign up in the first month. Open source as a business works.

choices.title: Keep it pure, find sponsors
choices.body: You add a sponsors page and approach companies using the tool. 5 sponsors at $500/month each.

choices.title: Get overwhelmed by the agent PRs
choices.body: Agent-submitted PRs flood in faster than you can review. You're now a bottleneck in your own project.

title: The Platform Risk
body: Anthropic changes their API pricing. Your AI costs triple overnight. You built your entire stack on Claude and now they own your economics. This is platform risk — the thing everyone warns about and nobody avoids because the tools are too good. You have 48 hours before the new billing kicks in. Your product's margins just went negative.

choices.title: Migrate to a different AI provider
choices.body: You spend 3 brutal days migrating to a cheaper model. Quality drops 15%. Costs drop 70%. You survive.

choices.title: Negotiate an enterprise deal with them
choices.body: You email their sales team. Your usage justifies a custom plan. They offer 40% off.

choices.title: Pass the cost to customers
choices.body: You raise prices by $10. Some churn. Most stay. But the precedent is set: your pricing is hostage to someone else's API.

title: Trust After Getting Burned
body: After the scam, you're paranoid about every new opportunity. An actual legitimate investor reaches out. Their fund is real. Their portfolio is impressive. But every DM looks like a trap now. The psychological cost of getting scammed isn't the money — it's the permanent suspicion that rewires your trust circuits.

choices.title: Verify everything, proceed cautiously
choices.body: You spend a week verifying them. They're real. The deal is real. Your paranoia saved you from bad deals and almost killed a good one.

choices.title: Trust your gut, take the meeting
choices.body: Your gut says real. You take the meeting. They invest. Sometimes the gut is right.

choices.title: Pass on all investors, bootstrap only
choices.body: No more outside money. No more trust exercises. You grow on revenue alone.

title: The Return
body: You took time away. You touched grass. You slept 8 hours for the first time in a year. Now you're back, and the product is still here, and your users are still paying. But the landscape shifted while you were gone. Two new AI-native competitors launched. The market moved. You're rested and behind. The treadmill doesn't pause.

choices.title: Come back focused, set sustainable pace
choices.body: You establish a 40-hour work week. For the first time. The product grows anyway. Slower, but it grows.

choices.title: Come back energized, ship fast to catch up
choices.body: The break gave you clarity. You ship the features the new competitors have, plus two they don't.

choices.title: Come back and immediately overwork again
choices.body: Old habits. You're back to 14-hour days within a week. The sabbatical was a comma, not a period.

title: The Burn Rate Crisis
body: Your costs grew faster than your revenue. AI tools, a contractor, server upgrades, that domain renewal you forgot about. Your MRR is $5K but your burn is $6K. You're losing $1,000 a month. The cruel irony: AI tools are what let you build this, and AI tool subscriptions are what's killing your margins.

choices.title: Cut costs ruthlessly
choices.body: You cancel half your AI subscriptions, fire the contractor, and go back to doing everything yourself with one model.

choices.title: Grow revenue faster than costs
choices.body: You launch a higher-priced tier. Three customers upgrade. The math starts working again.

choices.title: Take on debt to bridge the gap
choices.body: You put $3,000 on the credit card. It buys 3 months. The interest rate is 24.99%.

title: The Near-Zero Moment
body: Your bank account hits $247. You have 3 days until the next customer payment cycle. Your AI tool subscriptions auto-bill tomorrow. You're doing mental math about which tool to let lapse — the one that writes your code or the one that handles your customers. Sophie's choice but for SaaS subscriptions.

choices.title: Ask someone for a bridge loan
choices.body: You ask a friend for $1,000. They send it immediately. No questions. You cry in the bathroom.

choices.title: Hustle for quick revenue
choices.body: You offer annual plans at a 50% discount. Three customers buy. $1,400 hits your account in time.

choices.title: Let the AI tools lapse, go manual
choices.body: You cancel the AI subscriptions. For one week you code by hand. It takes 10x longer. You remember what it was like before.

title: The Accidental Funding Round
body: An angel investor sees your $10K MRR post and DMs: 'Can we talk?' One coffee turns into three meetings. They want to invest $100K at a $1M valuation. But here's the new wrinkle: they also want you to promise never to hire humans. 'AI-native or nothing,' they say. The money is real. The constraint is philosophical. Zero employees forever.

choices.title: Take the money, accept the constraint
choices.body: You take the $100K and the AI-native pledge. No humans. Just you and the machines. It's lonely and profitable.

choices.title: Negotiate away the no-humans clause
choices.body: You counter: take the money, keep the option to hire. They agree. Flexibility preserved.

choices.title: Decline, stay bootstrapped forever
choices.body: You say no. Nobody tells you how to run your company. You'll grow slower but you'll grow free.

title: Building Is Free Now
body: Building is free. Shipping is free. Marketing is free. An AI agent can conceive, build, launch, and market a product in 90 minutes for $0.03 in compute. The only scarce things left are ATTENTION and TRUST. Your entire career was built on the premise that building is hard. Building is no longer hard. You're a master locksmith in a world where all the doors disappeared.

choices.title: Pivot to attention and trust brokering
choices.body: You become a curator. You don't build — you select, endorse, and vouch. Your taste is the product now.

choices.title: Build anyway, it's who you are
choices.body: Building is free but it's still what makes you feel alive. You build for the act, not the outcome.

choices.title: Grieve the old world, quietly
choices.body: The world you trained for is gone. You sit with the loss. It's not dramatic. It's just Tuesday.

title: Everyone Is a Founder Now
body: AI tools made it so anyone can ship a product in an hour. Your Uber driver has three SaaS products. Your barista has a landing page with $2K MRR. The barrier to entry hit zero and the market flooded with 10 million micro-products. 'Founder' isn't a dream anymore — it's a default. Like having an email address.
